en: In the *Buddhabhāṣita-apramāṇa-mahāmaitrī-śāsana-sūtra*, it is said:
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, only those sentient beings who are icchantikas are difficult to transform and difficult to nurture.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied, "It is like an ox plowing a field; it is dispatched by the person [who uses it]."
The monkey’s dancing was due to being taught by a person;
sentient beings who commit transgressions are due to being incited by others.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
World-Honored One,
if there are sentient beings who are born in the western land as a result of my medicine,
I shall not decline even to offer my own body, nor my impurities from my mouth and eyes, as objects for their reliance.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"If there are sentient beings who diligently recite this sūtra of the Great Sage,
they shall escape the suffering of the three calamities."
First, those difficult to restrain who are prisoners;
second, those difficult to cure who are the sick;
third, those difficult to escape who are in hell.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed him, saying: "Ānanda,
it is because the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa are difficult to transform and difficult to nurture."
I shall open this treasury of sūtras and bring forth its extraordinary contents;
I will expound this wondrous sūtra for you.
If anyone reveals this sūtra, they will not give rise to pure faith.
You should know that such a person shares no karmic bond with me;
they extensively expound the sublime words of all the sutras to guide and deliver sentient beings.
Whoever utters my name once shall hear me and see me;
I will go to their rescue according to the sound of their cry.
Those who in this life skin and flay their preceptors or monastics will die and fall into the Cold Ice Hell;
furthermore, they will be born among silkworms to be boiled and skinned by others.
Such beings remain there for eighty thousand kalpas.
The remainder received the bodies of animals;
having passed through five hundred kalpas,
they became all manner of wriggling and moving sentient beings.
Thereafter, when receiving a human body,
he will be deformed, blind, and lame;
for five hundred kalpas, he will constantly suffer the retribution of being mute.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied, "Ānanda,
a nun who has practiced impure conduct dies and falls into the Iron Cave Hell."
Eighty thousand sword-wheels descended all at once,
severing his body.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"As the Buddha has considered,
this matter transcends the three realms.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Ānanda:
"Those who die intoxicated and deranged from drinking alcohol fall into the Copper-Drinking Hell.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One..."
"Since alcohol has no fixed destiny,
for what reason is it prohibited?
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again to Ānanda.
Intoxicated by drinking wine,
one does not recognize one's elders or kin.
I have seen people in the land of China who, because of wine, commit incest with their own mothers.
They violate the five precepts;
therefore, they are restrained.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke to the great bodhisattvas and others.
Since my attainment of Buddhahood until now,
more than five hundred kalpas have passed;
the sutras have been extensively expounded.
Having recited it completely,
he had never before heard these words,
nor had he ever heard this teaching.
If there are sentient beings who hear this sutra,
they have planted seeds of wholesome causes in the past and reaped the fruits of those wholesome causes in the past.
Reflecting upon this sutra,
it is inconceivable and beyond all measure.
At that time, the Tathāgata said to the bodhisattvas:
"The words I have spoken are as heavy as Mount Tai."
Sentient beings who hear it will regard it as light as a mote of dust.
This Dharma is difficult to hear and likewise difficult to see.
Thus spoke the Buddha to Ānanda.
If there are sentient beings who hear this sutra and feel joy and admiration in their hearts,
one should explain it to such people with all one's heart.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again to Ānanda:
"I see sentient beings falling into the three miserable realms;
it is as if they were being cut with a blade."
My body may endure this through it;
however, I cannot bear to see sentient beings undergoing great suffering and affliction.
Out of sorrowful compassion, I endure this pain.
Light emanates from his body,
illuminating the ten directions;
those with whom I have a karmic connection are able to see my body.
"One who is without conditions does not perceive the notion of a self. At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, what are these two kinds of mind?"
"A certain class of sentient beings has vision,
while another class lacks vision.
At that time, the Tathāgata spoke again to Ānanda.
"The sun and moon shine everywhere,
yet the blind do not see them.
At that time, Ānanda spoke again.
World-Honored One,
what is blindness?
What is clarity?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied, "Ānanda,
those who cultivate merit are wise."
"One who does not cultivate merit is blind.
Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One..."
"One who cultivates merit does not see by means of what.
The World-Honored One told Ānanda,
"One who cultivates merit does not see my body."
They obstruct and close off the Buddha’s light and defile the Three Jewels;
for this reason, they are unable to see me.
Thus spoke the Buddha to the bodhisattvas.
Those who hear this sutra will experience joy in their hearts,
like a child seeing his mother return from a long journey,
or like one who is hungry obtaining food, or one who is thirsty obtaining a drink.
For such a person, one should explain this with all one's heart.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Those who eat meat are like a pack of dogs."
The bones are contended over by each individual, who greedily views them;
the pigs and sheep constantly harbor thoughts of slaughter as they gaze upon them;
and the stinking flesh is like a cat pouncing on a mouse.
Those who possess a compassionate mind and apply their intent,
and who now believe in and understand the Buddha-dharma in this very life,
have come from among human beings.
Those who do not believe in the Buddha in their present life have come from among the animals;
those who commit offenses and do not repent them [will likewise fall].
It is like using gold to fill a country and thereby depleting one's own treasures; yet,
for one who has committed an offense and repents, it is like a sick person obtaining medicine and being restored to health,
or like stained undergarments being washed and becoming pure once again.
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Puguang:
"One who acts according to my words shall attain Buddhahood through a single verse;
one who does not believe me is like someone seeking a needle in the ocean."
It is said that they exhaust their efforts in vain without attaining realization.
The Buddha spoke to the bodhisattvas:
"Those who, in this present life, steal the property of others..."
In a future life, one will become a foolish ox for others, subjected to their cruel beatings;
through such untimely suffering,
one receives the body of an ox and remains a slave to others for five hundred kalpas.
To allow the mind to be driven at will is to suffer the punishment of being caught after having fled;
it is to have one's face marked and to undergo irrational, agonizing restraint.
The Buddha said to the bodhisattva:
"Within the *gāra*, there are two kinds of mind:
the first is the wholesome mind."
Second is an evil mind.
What constitutes an evil person?
It refers to any sentient being who, upon entering a temple, [acts with such intent].
They beg and solicit only from the Saṃgha;
they may seek out the faults of the monks or consume their offerings of merit with total lack of shame.
Carrying cakes, fruits, and vegetables in their arms, they return home.
Such a person dies and falls into the Iron Fork Hell;
how can they be called a virtuous person?
If there are sentient beings who enter a temple at such a time...
Seeing the Sangha, one pays them respect;
seeing the Buddha, one prostrates;
and one receives the precepts and performs repentance.
They relinquish wealth and property to sustain the Triple Gem,
not sparing even their own bodies or lives.
Those who uphold the Great Dharma—
such people, with every single step they take,
naturally proceed to the heavens to receive their rewards.
Regarding Jyotiṣka:
Jyotiṣka was indeed named the most excellent of virtuous men.
The Buddha addressed the great assembly:
Regarding the various causes and effects I have discussed, this sutra is distinguished by its name in two ways:
first, by its specific designation;
second, by its excellence.
The three Bodhisattvas said:
"If there are sentient beings who hear this sutra,
even those who give rise to a single thought of goodness shall be reborn in the Pure Land."
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva:
"Those who hear my teaching will give rise to joy in their hearts,
like one who finds water in a drought."
The young crops will revive and flourish;
those who do not accept my words are like stones submerged in water,
never receiving any moisture.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
do you see the land of China?"
Suppose there is a person who cultivates merit from the age of seven until the end of a hundred years,
yet at the moment of death breaks the five precepts.
Will this person obtain the fruit of their merit?
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again to Ānanda:
"It is like a chariot with solid hubs ascending a slope ten thousand *li* long."
When the carriage overturns upon reaching the precipice,
what loss could possibly have a fixed limit?
Even if one were to take some small portion of it, it would be like a shadow in the clouds.
The light of a single moment of the sun is like a mouthful of food that can provide long-lasting satiety;
thus the Buddha spoke to sentient beings.
We shall extensively explain the common causes and conditions for attaining Buddhahood together,
universally exhorting all sentient beings to collectively cultivate pure conduct.
All those in the world— gods, humans, asuras, and others—
having heard what the Buddha had spoken,
were all greatly rejoiced, paid their respects, and departed.
The Sūtra on the Teaching of Immeasurable Great Compassion Spoken by the Buddha, in one fascicle.
